title: Chapter 8 — The Principle Of Equality Suggests To The Americans The Idea Of The Indefinite Perfectibility Of Man
paragraphs: Idea of the Indefinite Perfectibility of Man

Equality suggests to the human mind several ideas that would not have come from any other source, and it modifies almost all the ideas held before. I take as an example the idea of human perfectibility, because it is one of the principal notions the intellect can conceive, and because it is in itself a great philosophical theory, whose consequences can be traced at every moment in the conduct of human affairs. Man has many points of resemblance with the animals, but one characteristic belongs to him alone: he improves, and they cannot. Mankind could not fail to notice this difference from its earliest period. The idea of perfectibility is therefore as old as the world. Equality did not give birth to it, though it has given it a new character.

When the citizens of a community are classed by rank, profession, or birth, and when everyone is forced to follow whatever career happens to open before him, each person thinks that the utmost limits of human power lie close at hand, and no one seeks any longer to resist the inevitable law of his destiny. It is not that an aristocratic people absolutely denies man’s capacity for self-improvement, but they do not hold it to be indefinite. They conceive of improvement, but not of change. They imagine that the future condition of society may be better, but not essentially different. And while they admit that mankind has made vast strides in improvement and may still have some to make, they fix certain impassable limits for it in advance. Thus they do not presume that they have reached the supreme good or absolute truth (what people or what person was ever foolish enough to imagine that?), but they are convinced that they have pretty nearly reached the degree of greatness and knowledge that our imperfect nature allows. Since nothing moves around them, they are willing to fancy that everything is in its proper place. Then it is that the legislator pretends to lay down eternal laws, that kings and nations will raise only monuments meant to last forever, and that the present generation undertakes to spare future generations the task of regulating their own destinies.

As castes disappear and the classes of society draw closer together, as mores, customs, and laws change through the tumultuous contact of people with one another, as new facts arise, as new truths come to light, as ancient opinions fade and others take their place, the image of an ideal perfection, always on the wing, presents itself to the human mind. Continual changes then occur at every moment under everyone’s eyes. The position of some is made worse, and he learns only too well that no people and no individual, however enlightened, can claim to be infallible. The condition of others is improved, and from this he infers that man is endowed with an indefinite capacity for improvement. His setbacks teach him that no one may hope to have found absolute good; his successes spur him to pursue it without end. Thus, always seeking, always falling to rise again, often disappointed but not discouraged, he moves unceasingly toward that immeasurable greatness, so dimly visible at the end of the long road that humanity has yet to travel. It is hard to believe how many facts flow naturally from the philosophical theory of the indefinite perfectibility of man, or how strong an influence it has even on people who live entirely for action and not for thought, and who seem to conform their actions to it without knowing anything about it. I stop an American sailor and ask why the ships of his country are built to last such a short time. He answers without hesitation that the art of navigation is making such rapid progress every day that the finest vessel would become almost useless if it lasted beyond a certain number of years. In these words, which fell by chance and on a particular subject from a man of rough education, I recognize the general and systematic idea on which a great people directs all its affairs.
Aristocratic nations are naturally too apt to narrow the scope of human perfectibility; democratic nations, to expand it beyond all limits.
